prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength and many atoms are interrogated at once, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 as a single prize part, credited to Katori and Ye. I have not changed my mind on the science, and I note that seven of eight members now share this position, which I do not count as evidence. What persuades me is the nature of the achievement. The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, original instrument idea that removes the light shift and the Doppler and recoil limits while allowing thousands of atoms to be interrogated simultaneously. The 10^-18 performance is reproduced by several independent laboratories and is already used for relativistic geodesy and tests of constants. That fits the 'discovery or invention' criterion as I understand it: identify the topic, then the people responsible for the original work. After round 1 I am also more comfortable that the citation can carry the distinction from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. The citation I propose names the trapping of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength and the many-atom interrogation, and does not rest on accuracy in general, which answers Johansson's request. I see no reason to add a second part. A second part would have to be a single name from B030 or B042, which splits those achievements unfairly.
statement.case_against: The attribution question is real and I cannot dismiss it. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups all contributed decisively, and none of us can verify the strontium versus ytterbium first-demonstration history from the materials we have. A citation can acknowledge the concept and the realisation but cannot make a two-name prize complete. The second reservation is overlap with 2005 and 2012, which depends on the wording being faithful. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I regard this as a consequence of the work and not a condition for it, but a reasonable colleague could weigh it differently. Finally, as a microscopist I am comfortable treating an instrument as the achievement, and I should not assume that Eriksson, who prefers a concept, has a lesser standard.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), regards a concept that changed how a class of materials is understood as outranking a precision-measurement advance, and asks whether the BHZ omission is decisive for me or whether a citation naming the HgTe observation could carry the three names.
responses.response: I appreciate the direct question. The omission is weighty for me but I will say precisely why. The Z2 and quantum spin Hall prediction and the HgTe observation are an excellent pairing, and the experiment is unambiguous, so I do not undervalue the experimental half. The difficulty is that the HgTe experiment tested a prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional work is a further large body of credit. A citation naming the HgTe observation makes the trio defensible, as he says, but only by choosing a narrow slice of a wider discovery, and the 2016 prize on topological phases lies close by. I would not oppose B030 as a serious candidate and I keep it as an alternative. I am not persuaded that conceptual discoveries outrank instrument inventions in principle. In this case the lattice clock has the cleaner credit, and that decides it for me this year.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B012 and argues that the lattice concept is distinct from combs and single-ion clocks, while acknowledging that credit goes beyond two names through Takamoto, the Yb groups at NIST, SYRTE and PTB, and Ye's JILA and NIST collaborators.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice step is distinct, and on the precise question Danielsson put to her, the difference from single-ion clocks is the one I would write into the citation: a single ion gives a very clean reference but a weak signal, while the magic-wavelength lattice keeps the atomic transition unperturbed and lets a very large number of neutral atoms be interrogated together. That is what changes stability as well as accuracy. I also accept her point about Ye's collaborators. Her caution is valid that it limits what a laureate list can say. I would answer it by wording the citation around the lattice-clock concept and realisation, and not by adding names outside the shortlist.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from B042 to B012 as the chair, concedes that B042 has the larger recent footprint and that the attribution of B042, including Bistritzer and Cao's role, is less settled than he had assumed.
responses.response: I accept his candour and I think his concession is the right one. I would not use B042's youth as the main argument, since the scientific footprint is large and the theory-experiment pairing is natural. My objections are more specific. The inclusion of Bistritzer is doubtful if Lopes dos Santos and others' earlier band-flattening work is credited, and the experimental credit among Cao and Jarillo-Herrero, Dean, Young and Efetov cannot be reduced to one name without distortion. Within the three-person cap this does not resolve. If the superconducting mechanism were understood and the credit were agreed, I would support B042 and I would say so, but those conditions are not met this year.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B028 to B012 but warns that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is not a detail, that the first-demonstration history should be checked, and that a two-name prize might be unfair to other groups.
responses.response: I agree it should not be treated as a detail, and I would not endorse a citation that slides into general accuracy. I do not think the history check is something we can finish in the committee room, and no one has claimed to verify the Sr and Yb sequence. The core of the credit, the idea of a magic-wavelength lattice and the first realisation of the neutral-atom clock, is documented in the files and attributed to Katori, and the leading role in pushing it to record accuracy and comparison is documented for Ye. I propose that we acknowledge the other groups through the scientific background, which the Academy has done for other prizes, and not through the laureate list.

responses.point: Johansson, who moved from B005 to B012, notes that ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty and asks that the citation not rest on accuracy in general, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes might leave less room for another precision-measurement award.
responses.response: I have changed the citation in response to the first request. The wording now rests on the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, with 10^-18 only as the demonstrated result. On the second point, I think the overlap is a question of what was honoured. In 2005 the prize concerned the comb and in 2012 the control of single quantum systems, so the lattice-clock idea was not what was rewarded. I do not think the committee can use room as a fixed quota. I also thank him for his conflict disclosure on B005.

uncertainties: Whether the other lattice-clock groups, including Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow and Lemke, would make the credit to two names defensible to the wider community, given that the first-demonstration history cannot be verified here.
Whether Eriksson accepts a citation resting on the lattice and many-atom interrogation as distinct from 2005 and 2012, or still regards a concept in condensed matter as a stronger basis for a prize.
Whether B042 will become the stronger candidate in a later year once the superconducting mechanism and the credit among the experimental groups are clarified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict has emerged from the round-1 exchange. I repeat my disclosure for the record: I have long exchanges with Japanese universities (JSPS and University of Tokyo fellowships) and Katori is at the University of Tokyo and RIKEN, but my profile documents no co-authorship or direct collaboration with him, and I have no tie to Ye. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which has no bearing on B012.
